title: G-D-L
hookLine: gadol, gedulah: great, and to grow

cards: Pencil marks climb a kitchen doorframe, each one with a name and a date. Nobody saw the child get taller between the marks. It happened at night, at school, over cereal.
Then one day the mark is above the parent's shoulder. In Hebrew, growing and great share a root. Gadal, he grew.
Gadol, great, big. A gadol can be a grown-up, or a towering teacher. Being great and getting bigger are one family of words.

teach.h: THE CHILD: AND THE CHILD GREW.
teach.b: Turn this root four ways. First, the child. When Isaac, the long-awaited son, gets bigger, the Torah marks it simply: "And the child grew, and was weaned."
And Abraham throws a great feast. The same root twice in one verse: the child grows, the feast is great. Growing is worth celebrating.

teach.h: THE PROMISE: GREAT, TO BE A BLESSING.
teach.b: Second, the promise: "I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing." The sentence lands not on great, but on blessing.
Some readers hear in it that being made great is for the sake of being a blessing. Third, the grown-up.

teach.h: THE GROWN-UP: HE LOOKED ON THEIR BURDENS.
teach.b: Moses is raised in Pharaoh's palace, and then: "when Moses was grown up, that he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." What the grown Moses does is step outside and look at someone else's load.
Growing up, in this verse, looks outward.
Fourth, the prayer. The Kaddish, which you met on day six hundred three, opens with this root: yitgadal, may God's name grow great. Can God get bigger?
Some teachers answer that it asks for God's greatness to grow in the world, in how people see and live.
And mourners say it in a season when their own world may seem to have grown smaller. So G-D-L holds a child, a promise, a grown man and a prayer. In each, greatness isn't sitting still.

how: The Kaddish, recited in synagogue services and by mourners, begins with yitgadal, from the root G-D-L, asking that God's name grow great; in Jewish speech a gadol can mean a great Torah scholar.

o: a root for growing, and so for being great
a root for a fence, a wall around a garden
a root for cutting, as in cutting down a tree

s: in Hebrew, great and to grow come from different roots
gadal, he grew, and gadol, great, share the root G-D-L.
God's promise to Abraham ends on greatness
it ends on blessing: "and be thou a blessing."
the Kaddish opens with a word from this root
yitgadal, may God's name grow great.

games.q: you're Moses, grown up in Pharaoh's palace. what do you do, in the story?
o: go out to your brethren and look on their burdens.
games.why: "he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." growing up, here, looks outward.

practice: Think of one thing in your reach that's growing, or trying to: a plant on a windowsill, a child learning to read, a new coworker finding their feet, a friendship that needs one more conversation.
Picture the next small thing you could do for it, water, patience, a question, and imagine the next mark on the doorframe; if you pray, bring its name, or theirs, into the quiet.
And if a loss is weighing on you today, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: G-D-L. Gimel, dalet, lamed: the root of gadal, to grow, and gadol, great, and of yitgadal, the first word of the Kaddish. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he grew, became great; gadol means great.

carryVoice: Your line: grow. In Hebrew, great is something that is still growing. Until tomorrow, then.
